10853-our-gift: A Boston gift book of 1851, published by Abel Tompkins of Cornhill and entered for copyright in 1850. Its dedication verses promise no borrowed glories or flowers of language, only a simple, pure offering, a wreath of wild roses watered by love's gentle showers. Tears for the early dead and a humble moral entwined with affection set its tone.
11439-the-snow-drop-a-holiday-gift:
Miss Sarah S. Mower's 1851 Snow-Drop, a holiday gift, was written by an authoress described in its preface as misfortune's child. disease in early childhood deprived her of schooling and intercourse, and for six years she could seldom leave home. Winds through groves around her father's retired dwelling, songsters caroling, and the Androscoggin's ripple inspired her artless strains. written to beguile tedious time and offered to the benevolent public for pastime and moral sentiment.

The title poem praises a sweet, unassuming flower that dares rear its head before April showers, without purple, scarlet, blue, or gold display. The book's pathos and modesty are its appeal. For readers of women's and disability history, it documents authorship from confinement.
12743-the-author-s-craft:
Arnold Bennett's 1914 book on writing divides into two parts: Seeing Life and Writing Novels. He argues that a novelist must first learn to observe people closely, then turn that sight into form, character, and story. Examples range from Balzac and Flaubert to Dostoevsky and Maupassant, praised and faulted with equal frankness.

Bennett warns that fine technique alone cannot save a book whose mind is thin, and that clumsy masters can still tower over neat craftsmen. His tone is that of a working novelist talking shop. The book suits aspiring writers who want practical counsel rather than lofty theory.
14418-thrift:
Samuel Smiles published this London volume in 1892 as a follow-up to his earlier works on self-help and character. It treats thrift as a moral habit, not mere penny-pinching, and links honest earning, careful spending, and steady saving to independence and family security.

Chapters move through industry, waste, debt, insurance, and the temptations of speculation, drawing on lives of workers, clerks, and small traders. Smiles argues that small sums set aside regularly can lift a household out of want. The book still reads as a Victorian manual of prudence, duty, and self-respect.
14461-letters-on-demonology-and-witchcra:
Sir Walter Scott wrote these letters in 1830 for Murray's Family Library, and this 1884 edition reprints them with an introduction by Henry Morley. Scott, the novelist, turns historian of superstition.

He traces fairy belief, ghosts, witch trials, and demon lore from ancient times through the Scottish persecutions, weighing what people believed against what evidence supports. Stories of the Isle of Man, Norse spirits, and village wise women fill the pages. The letters argue for reason and humanity, and they remain a readable survey of how fear shaped law and legend. Scott's cool tone keeps even grim trials readable.
1463-the-private-papers-of-henry-ryecrof:
Presented as papers left by a retired writer, this quiet book gathers Henry Ryecroft's notes from a cottage in the English countryside. After years of hard literary labour in London, Ryecroft lives simply, reads, walks, and sets down thoughts on books, seasons, old friends, and the small pleasures of a settled day.

The entries move by mood rather than by plot, from a sunrise to a memory of cheap lodgings and lentil soup. Their charm is their honesty about age, work, and contentment. Readers who love slow, reflective prose will find a companion here, and a portrait of a mind at peace.
1669-the-human-drift:
Jack London's Human Drift gathers essays and sketches from the 1919 Mills and Boon edition, opening with the title essay on the revelations of devout and learned men. Moving through small-boat sailing, four horses and a sailor, and a classic of the sea. A wicked woman curtain raiser and a birth mark sketch close the set.

London writes of work, wandering, and the sea with his usual force, mixing philosophy with yarns of ships and men. The collection is uneven but vivid. It offers London the essayist and storyteller together, for readers who know his novels and want his shorter pieces.
17767-pee-wee-harris-adrift:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade, Roy Blakeley, and Pee-Wee Harris books, wrote this boys' adventure, published by Grosset and Dunlap with pictures by H. S. Barbour and the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. A frontispiece shows Pee-Wee rowing his customers to Alligator Island. Chapters open with Pee-Wee alone, Saturday morning, and castles in the air.

Keekie Joe, a question of duty, and the missionary follow, with apple blossom time, Pee-Wee exploring the island, and a lookout seeing a sail ahead. Readers get a Scout story of pluck, humour, and island adventure, in Fitzhugh's lively style. The book suits young readers of Scout fiction.
21929-a-master-of-craft:
A pretty girl stands on a Wapping jetty at evening in W. W. Jacobs's novel A Master of Craft, published in 1899. Below her rests the schooner Foam, her galley cold and her hatches closed against the quiet Thames. The girl puts a small foot toward the rigging, thinking of the jump down. She wants Captain Flower, who went ashore half an hour before.

A young man hurries up, and the tale of the Foam begins. Jacobs stretches his short-story gifts across a full novel of sailors, courtship, and craft. Fraser, in the talk quoted at the front, wonders why the captain never mentioned the girl's dark eyes. The master of craft of the title has more to master than his ship. It is Jacobs afloat and ashore at once.
22800-mary-wollstonecraft:
Mary Wollstonecraft is a biography of the great feminist pioneer, published in 1884, when her reputation still needed rescue. The catalog record names no author. Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, had been dead nearly ninety years, and respectable opinion still treated her life as a scandal.

Few women, the biographer begins, worked so faithfully for humanity's cause. Few drew such bitter censure, either. She gave herself to relieving suffering fellow beings with a saint's ardor. In return, people called her a moral scourge of God. The biography argues her case with documents and sympathy. It stands near the head of the long effort that restored Wollstonecraft to her place in history.
22822-the-superstitions-of-witchcraft:
Howard Williams, a scholar with an M.A., surveys the long history of witchcraft belief in The Superstitions of Witchcraft. Dreams, magic terrors, miracles, witches, ghosts, and portents all crowd his opening pages. Williams stresses that such fears were not confined to remote ages or to the so-called dark ages of Europe.

He finds the clearest proof much closer to his own time. The laws, theology, and popular prejudice of the seventeenth century supply case after case of accusation and punishment. By tracing how educated people endorsed the panic, Williams turns a lurid subject into social history. The book suits readers who want the witch trials explained as a product of belief, law, and fear together.
24579-woodcraft:
Nessmuk, the pen name of George Washington Sears, wrote this classic of outdoor life, on woodcraft and camping. Its first chapter treats overwork and recreation, outing and outers, and how to do it. Nessmuk quotes Herbert Spencer on Americans as an over-worked nation, whose hair turns gray ten years earlier than an Englishman's.

Later chapters teach camp life: what to carry, how to travel light, and how to enjoy the woods without burden. Nessmuk writes with humour and practical wisdom for tired city workers. His book remains a beloved guide to simple camping, and a founding text of American outdoor writing.
24842-the-defence-of-duffer-s-drift:
The Defence of Duffer's Drift first ran in the Journal of the United States Infantry Association, volume one, number four, April 1905, copyrighted 1904. It teaches small-unit tactics through a story: a young officer must hold a drift, a river crossing, against attack, and he learns by hard trial what works and what fails.

Each lesson is stated plainly. One warning says a shallow trench with a low parapet can be worse than useless, since it gives gunners a mark and no shield from shrapnel. Scattering men in grass, bush, and behind stones may serve better. Soldiers still read it as a classic on thinking clearly under fire and learning from one's own mistakes.
24859-turned-adrift:
Harry Collingwood wrote Turned Adrift, a fast-moving sea tale that opens with the seizure of the clipper Zenobia. Built for speed on the London to Natal passenger run, the barque of 376 tons is taken on the night of January 24, 1862, in the South Atlantic. Her crew must then fend for themselves far from land.

Later chapters show castaway ingenuity, including a makeshift diving dress of oiled canvas sewn to keep water out. Collingwood, a master of nautical writing, keeps the pace brisk and the seamanship exact. Readers who like sea adventure will enjoy a tale of capture, survival, and clever work with poor tools.
26277-margarita-s-soul-the-romantic-reco:
Ingraham Lovell's Margarita's Soul, issued in London and New York in 1909, tells the romantic recollections of a man of fifty. Its eight parts follow a stream from a secret spring to a river in rapids, with fate as the guide at every turn. Chapters promise fate walking Broadway, fate going fishing, Roger finding an island, and Margarita meeting the enemy and making him hers.

Margarita, olive-skinned with chestnut hair, bathes in Seine water and becomes a pearl of too great price. An island cottage, an island feast, and an island tomb mark the course of love. The narrator looks back on Eden summers and a second summer in Eden, with fate casting dice, spreading nets, and laughing at his hopes.
3091-the-giant-raft:
Jules Verne wrote The Giant Raft as an Amazon adventure in two parts, Eight Hundred Leagues on the Amazon and The Cryptogram. The Garral family travels downriver on a jangada, a giant raft village, from Iquitos to Pevas and the frontier. Chapters on a captain of the woods, robber and robbed, hesitation, a forest on the ground, and following a liana mark the way to Ega. Fragoso and Torres join the voyage with secrets.

Verne pauses for natural history, explaining that braza, burning embers, gave brazil for dye woods and then Brazil for the vast equatorial district where those woods grow. The raft journey mixes geography, botany, and a criminal mystery solved by a cryptogram. The novel remains a classic Verne voyage, educational and exciting in equal measure.
33811-the-pearl-of-love-or-josey-s-gift:
Mrs. Madeline Leslie writes a children's moral tale in this Boston book, entered for copyright in 1868 and dedicated to the children of D. F. Appleton of New York. Its text, love is the fulfilling of the law, frames eight chapters following little red-cheeked Josey Codman. These include Josey's ride, the two nurses, the wrong baby, Josey's temper, Josey's Christmas, the burned baby, Josey's sorrow, and Josey's gift.

The opening shows Josey begging to ride with his mother, while Aunt Fanny urges that he can sit between them and be no trouble, and baby Emma dislikes her wrappings. Through small domestic incidents, Leslie teaches love, temper, and generosity in the plain, affectionate style of her Bible Pearls series. Young readers and historians of children's literature will find a sweet, earnest example of nineteenth-century moral storytelling.
34235-spun-yarn-and-spindrift:
Norah M. Holland's 1918 book Spun-Yarn and Spindrift gathers poems of Ireland, the sea, and the war years. Irish songs and tales sit beside sea songs, Christmas hymns, and verses for the dead of 1916 and 1917.

Holland also honours poets she admired, with pieces for W. B. Yeats and James Whitcomb Riley, and writes of airmen, sailors, and homes left behind. The poems are short, plain, and musical, moving between home, shore, and front. Holland's table of contents runs from dog-angels and fairy tales to ships, soldiers, and Christmas hymns.
34773-woodcraft:
E H Kreps wrote Woodcraft, a small book of hunting and trapping pieces published in New York in 1919. Elmer Kreps was born in Union County, Pennsylvania, in 1880, when game was plentiful near his home. From boyhood he loved the woods. The editor of Fur News introduces him as a keen observer, an artist, and a frequent writer on his craft.

The book collects his magazine articles, with pictures from his own sketches. The first piece tells how to build the home camp. Kreps recalls fixing up an old lumber camp and learning the worth of a double wall against winter cold. Later pieces share what he learned across the United States and Canada. The book aims to brighten the lives of trappers and hunters.
37447-hand-craft:
Hand Craft pages list drawing books for schools, with prices. The kindergarten drawing book in two parts was compiled by Rooper: part one in a small quarto at one shilling sixpence, and part two, on curved lines, at one shilling. Two hundred blackboard drawing exercises for infants' classes stand beside them.

Infants' drawing books, a varied occupation, run in three books at twopence each. Book one works vertical and horizontal lines of varying lengths in combination. Book two adds oblique lines at angles of forty five degrees, and book three turns to various angles. They were recommended by the Science and Art Department for beginning in elementary day schools. Junior drawing books in three books at twopence meet the requirements of the new class subject, drawing. A complete course in freehand and geometry is promised, with full directions and space for working.
38994-the-iron-boys-as-foremen-or-headin:
The Iron Boys as Foremen, published in 1912, is James Mears's mine story for boys, one of his Iron Boys books. Steve Rush and Bob Jarvis work the Red Rock Mine, riding the cage to the fifteenth level. Five strokes on the gong tell the cage-tender that men are coming up, so the steel cage must rise with care.

The chapter list promises a full shift of trouble. A tragedy in the shaft opens the tale, and a surprise promotion follows. Fire breaks out underground, and the boys win through tunnels of flame. A labor leader tempts them, miners meet in secret and demands are laid down. Mob vengeance and a cowardly blow test the young foremen.
40148-the-footlights-fore-and-aft:
Channing Pollock wrote The Footlights Fore and Aft, copyrighted in 1911 and published at Boston, with fifty full page illustrations by Warren Rockwell. The catalog dates it to 1911. Pollock's pieces first appeared in Collier's, the Saturday Evening Post, Munsey's, and the Smart Set. He dedicated the book to the lady who goes to the theater with him.

Pollock, a playwright and the leading American drama critic of his day, writes of the theater from both sides of the footlights. Actors, managers, press agents, and audiences all get chapters. A cartoon shows plays put up in packages and sold at delicatessen shops. His wit is professional and his knowledge first hand. The book is a backstage tour of Broadway and the road in 1911.
40170-the-romance-of-aircraft:
Romance of Aircraft, by Laurence Yard Smith, surveys flight for general readers. Grant Richards of London issued the book in nineteen nineteen with many photographs. Thirty three pictures and six diagrams support the text throughout the volume. Front views show Navy seaplanes NC one, three, and four at Rockaway.

Part one treats the conquest of the air and balloon craft of all kinds. Early balloon feats, the parachute, and Great War ballooning fill those chapters. Part two turns to the dirigible and its growth in war service. Part three covers heavier than air machines, first rules, and the pioneers. Famous Allied and German planes and heroes of the air follow.
41414-the-girl-from-the-marsh-croft:
Selma Lagerlöf, the Swedish novelist, wrote The Girl from the Marsh Croft, first published in English by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1910. A prefatory note warns readers that Lagerlöf had left her earlier romantic manner for a harder, more realistic kind of story.

The marsh croft is a poor smallholding, and its girl carries the shame and strain of a hard rural life. Lagerlöf follows her through disgrace toward a chance at respect, watching neighbors judge and relent. The tale shows the plainer style that won Lagerlöf wide fame in Sweden and, soon after, the Nobel Prize in Literature.
41532-swift:
Swift, by Leslie Stephen, is a life of Jonathan Swift in the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley. Macmillan and Company published the volume in London in 1882. Stephen builds the book chiefly on Swift's own writings and letters, and his preface sorts out the earlier lives on which any new one must rest.

The preface weighs Lord Orrery's Remarks of 1751, written by a man who had known Swift from about 1732 but cared more for showing his own taste than for accuracy. It then turns to Delany's Observations of 1754, which defended Swift against Orrery, and to the essay of 1756 by Deane Swift, a kinsman. Johnson's later life is judged slight. Stephen's method is to test each witness, then write a compact critical biography of the dean, satirist and author of Gulliver's Travels.
44021-feudal-england-historical-studies-:
Round first published these studies of feudal England in 1895, and the copy here is a later impression from 1909. The subject is England in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Round works from charters, Domesday records and court rolls, and he argues closely from small points of wording and date.

A note explains that names brought in only to illustrate an argument are left out of the index. The prefix Fitz, as in Geoffrey de Mandeville, is kept as a useful habit. Footnotes cite Belgian charter lists, the Fortnightly Review and the Quarterly Review, showing the scholarly debate behind the work.
44215-the-book-of-camp-lore-and-woodcraf:
The Book of Camp-Lore and Woodcraft, by Dan Beard, founder of the first Boy Scouts group, was issued in New York with 377 drawings by the author. The title page carries a 1920 copyright, and Beard dates his note December 1, 1930, from Suffern, New York. He dedicates the book to George Du Pont Pratt, a New York conservation leader.

Early chapters teach fire by friction, with full steps for the fire-board, bow, drill, and thimble, plus fire myths and record makers. Later parts cover flint and steel, how to lay a fire, and how to work in wet weather. Clear steps and lore make the book a hands-on guide for campers and scouts.
44289-an-outline-of-english-speech-craft:
William Barnes set out in 1878 to teach English grammar through English itself, without leaning on Greek or Latin words. Kegan Paul and Company published the little book in London, and Barnes calls his opening word a fore-say rather than a preface.

Speech, he argues, was made of breath-sounds for the ears of hearers, not of letters in books for the eyes. So consonants and vowels become breath-pennings and free-breathings, and spelling is left aside until the speech itself is learned. The lore-words of learning get plain English names, which a learner can hold in mind. Even grammar is a misused word, borrowed from writing. The verbs, his time-words, are sorted as weak or strong by their endings, a plan he offers as new.
44501-toy-craft:
Leon Baxter's Toy Craft was printed in 1922 by the Bruce Publishing Company of Milwaukee. Baxter directed manual training in the public schools of St Johnsbury, Vermont, and had written on bird houses and concrete work before. Two short notes at the front frame the aim of the book.

The aim is to give plain directions so that boys and girls can make their own toys: small furniture, wooden dolls, carts, and animals. A toy a child has put together, the notes argue, is worth far more than any number of factory goods. Mabel Turner, of the American Red Cross Junior Service, adds the second gain: the joy of making a thing for some other child.
44766-needlecraft:
Effie Archer Archer wrote this guide to work with the needle, printed in 1916. She was an editor of needle work for famed sheets, and did work with the schools of New York and with clubs of craft. The book is one of a set on work and play. A photo at the front shows the last step in the make of a button hole.

The first part starts with the box of tools. It tells what a girl should have in her work box, and how to sew on buttons. It goes on to the tack stitch, to the mend of a worn place, and to the stitch that runs back on itself. Hem work and the cast of an edge come in their turn.
4592-cast-adrift:
T. S. Arthur published Cast Adrift in 1873, calling it a romance of real life in which truth proves stranger than fiction. He says he lifted only part of the veil hiding victims of intemperance in large cities. There the fallen herd together like wild beasts. He presents his scenes as photographs from real life rather than pure invention. The book opens with an unwelcome babe, a defrauded young mother, and a hard struggle.

Later chapters follow Mrs. Dinneford's plans, a splendid boy, sympathy between father and daughter, and the rotten heart of a great city, with Pinky Swett at the mercy of a street crowd. Arthur writes with earnest moral force, aiming to stir Christian readers to pity and reform. Readers get a grim, plainspoken temperance novel, useful for the social history of its day, and a warning about how cities can swallow the friendless.
4944-scenes-and-characters-or-eighteen-m:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Scenes and Characters follows eighteen months at Beechcroft, centered on Eleanor Mohun, eldest child of a gentleman of old family and good property. Eleanor, quiet, steady, and useful, finds her chief pleasure in nursing and household duty, while cousins, a rector's illness, a little nephew, and a baronial court fill the chapters.

Chapter titles promise minor misfortunes, vanity and vexation, and charity beginning at home, all in Yonge's moral domestic mode. The novel's epigraph points to patient faith found in the daily round. Readers get a gentle chronicle of family life, where small trials test character more than great events do.
50498-the-raft:
Coningsby Dawson, author of The Garden Without Walls, wrote this novel, published at New York in 1914 with pictures by Orson Lowell. An old line heads it: their virgins had no marriage songs, and swimmers cast themselves into the sea. The title hints at shipwreck and survival.

The first chapter, A Man, opens on Jehane, a don's daughter at Oxford. She married blindly on the rebound, she later confessed, from dread of becoming an old maid. She and her friend Nan Tudor watch the undergraduates and fret over their fate. Dawson begins with Oxford comedy, though the raft of the title waits ahead, where marriage and danger will test his people at sea.
53067-color-cement-handicraft:
Pedro J Lemos and Reta A Lemos wrote Color Cement Handicraft, issued by the Davis Press at Worcester, Massachusetts, with copyright in nineteen twenty two. The pair gave the book to Robert B Harshe, director of the Chicago Art Institute, for his early help. Twenty chapters and many plates fill the manual. Foreword and colour plates in front set the tone. Tiles and pottery are the crafts taught.

Chapter one treats materials and equipment, and chapter two the making of plaster molds. Plain and incised tiles, vases and bowls, and colour in tiles follow. Relief tiles, majolica tiles, sgraffito work, and modeled and carved cement fill the middle. Glass mosaic tiles, flower boxes, garden work, candlesticks, and book supports close the craft side. Schoolroom projects and designing for tiles end the book. Craft teachers get a full workshop guide.
54371-with-force-and-arms-a-tale-of-love:
Howard R Garis wrote a tale of love and Salem witchcraft published at New York in 1908. A front picture shows a man drawing his sword and striking a door with its hilt. The title promises arms as well as romance. Garis later became famous for the Uncle Wiggily stories for children. This early book is a historical romance for older readers.

Salem's witch trials supply the dark backdrop for the love story. Garis sets swordplay and courtship amid the panic of 1692. Ogilvie issued many such popular novels from its Rose Street house. The tale joins a long line of fiction built on the Salem tragedy, mixing documented horror with invented heroes.
54426-modern-musical-drift:
Modern Musical Drift is a book of music criticism by W J Henderson, published by Longmans, Green and Company in 1904. Henderson wrote The Story of Music and other studies. He dedicates this one to his friend and colleague James Huneker, in a teasing poem of verse.

In the poem the dead masters watch the moderns from beside the Styx. Palestrina stares and Handel bemoans music's early death. Bach alone keeps calm, claiming he taught them how. The essays take up Wagner first. Parsifalia treats the first American Parsifal, given on a Christmas Eve. Three essays follow the Ring, and one treats Isolde's serving-woman. Richard Strauss gets four chapters, ending with the question of what it all means. Italian opera of today and the oratorio of today close the book.
56119-the-great-lord-burghley-a-study-in:
The Great Lord Burghley is a study in Elizabethan statecraft by Martin Hume, published in London in 1898. Hume had edited the calendars of Spanish state papers and wrote on the courtships of Queen Elizabeth. He dedicates the book to the Marquis of Salisbury, Burghley's descendant.

A Burghley saying heads the work: no man can be a good statesman who prizes his own gain over the public good. The text weighs Cecil's distrust of France and his care for Scotland and the Netherlands. It shows Elizabeth drawn back, again and again, to her minister's steady line. Readers get a close political life of the queen's chief adviser.
56430-the-race-of-the-swift:
Edwin Litsey wrote the Race of the Swift, for Little, Brown in 1905. Bull drew its illustrations from life for the Boston book. The gray fox was leading bravely, its frontispiece caption reads. Litsey had written the Love Story of Abner Stone before. Some tales here first ran in a monthly magazine's pages.

Others ran in a sporting magazine before the book gathered them. The author thanks those editors for leave to use the tales. Acknowledgment is made in the front pages of the volume. Swift wild things race through the stories of the set. Fox and hound and the creatures of field and stream fill them. October of 1905 saw the book published at Boston. Litsey gives the chase its short prose laureate in these tales.
56751-the-jolly-book-of-boxcraft:
Patten Beard wrote The Jolly Book of Boxcraft, printed in New York with rights held in 1914. Sixty-eight photos by North show models made by Beard herself. Twenty-three diagrams by Pattee go with them. She gives the book to all little children.

Boxville fronts the book, a whole town built of boxes. The craft turns pasteboard boxes into dolls' houses, shops, forts, and toys with a knife, paste, and paint. Beard thanks the children who taught her much of it. The book is a feast of making from the age before plastic. Young makers and their elders get a jolly, thorough guide.
58463-the-history-of-thomas-hickathrift:
The History of Thomas Hickathrift prints an old English chapbook tale from the earliest copies that survive, edited with an introduction by George Laurence Gomme. It was printed in London in 1885 for the Villon Society, as the first of a series of chapbooks and folk-lore tracts edited by Gomme and Wheatley. Gomme argues that Hickathrift may have been a real man of the Isle of Ely marsh country.

The tale makes its hero a brewer's man at Lynn who traded to Wisbeach and grew into a giant of folk story, strong enough to fight ogres. Chapbooks were the cheap print of the poor for centuries. This scholarly reprint saves one favourite for students of folk tale.
58627-bob-steele-in-strange-waters-or-ab:
Donald Grayson wrote Bob Steele in Strange Waters, or Aboard a Strange Craft. McKay published the submarine adventure at Philadelphia in 1909, under a Street and Smith copyright. Forty-eight chapters follow Bob Steele and the submarine Grampus from sealed orders at Belize. The run brings a mutiny, a hidden snare, and the capture of a general. The frontispiece shows the submarine battling a gigantic bull cachalot, and the plot runs down the coast, through the Gulf, and at last under the Amazon to Para.

The opening puts the captain and Bob in Saint George's Bay, ten miles from Belize, with 225 feet of water under the boat. Before opening the rest of the sealed orders, the captain means to test the Grampus to her warranted depth. Grayson bills himself as author of the famous motor-power stories. The book keeps that brisk series pace of dives, fights, and narrow margins.
58825-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Jonathan Swift is a finding list compiled by David Widger. Widger produced the volume for the Gutenberg collection. It gathers the contents of Swift's works held by the project. Each work's own table of contents follows in turn.

The list opens with The Battle of the Books and A Modest Proposal. The Bickerstaff-Partridge papers come next. The Journal to Stella and A Tale of a Tub follow. Several volumes of the prose works are indexed. Two volumes of the poems appear as well. Gulliver's Travels is listed in two forms. The Tale of a Tub contents show its famous digressions. Sermons and hints to servants round out the holdings.
59708-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Jonathan Swift is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. Like its companion volumes for other authors, it gathers the tables of contents of every Swift work then in the free library, so a reader can survey the whole shelf at once.

Gulliver's Travels leads, in two forms, one of them an illustrated edition with thirty eight illustrations and a map. Its contents begin with the voyage to Lilliput, where the shipwrecked author is made prisoner and carried up the country. Then come the Bickerstaff-Partridge Papers, the Tale of a Tub, two volumes of poems, and the Irish tracts. A Modest Proposal, the Journal to Stella, the Battle of the Books and the Drapier's Letters are all listed. Hints to Servants, the writings on religion, and three prayers and sermons close the roll of the Dean's works.
6014-west-wind-drift:
George Barr McCutcheon opens on a bright, still October morning, as the Doraine sails from a South American port with some seven hundred and fifty souls aboard. Her holds brim with grain, foodstuffs, metals, chemicals, rubber, and certain sinister things of war, bound for a port six thousand miles away.

Her passengers include men distinguished in finance, business, diplomacy, war, and adventure, from both hemispheres and all continents. Yet sly undersea monsters of German descent prowl the oceans, taking toll of humanity. McCutcheon sets a cosmopolitan company adrift toward danger on a wartime sea.
60980-remarks-of-the-president-in-presen:
Remarks of the President in Presenting to Madam Curie a Gift of Radium from the American People records a White House ceremony. The Government Printing Office at Washington printed the pamphlet in 1921. The remarks were delivered at three in the afternoon on May 20, 1921. The seal of the President heads the page. The President greets Madame Curie on behalf of the American nation.

He welcomes her as an adopted daughter of France, America's earliest supporter among the great nations. He greets her as a native-born daughter of Poland, newly restored to its rightful place. In her, he says, America honors a woman whose work has earned universal acclaim. She stands foremost among scientists in the age of science. The gift of radium, bought by American subscription, passed to her at this ceremony.
62530-adventures-in-thrift:
Adventures in Thrift, by Anna Steese Richardson with pictures by Charles Corson, was copyrighted in 1915 and published at Indianapolis in 1916 by Bobbs-Merrill. A proverb heads chapter one: luxury is attained through thrift. A plate shows a shopper exclaiming that she never weighed the pounds. The tale is a story of women, money, and the cost of living in the war years.

Chapter one opens in a department-store restaurant. One woman folds her veil with care, spears it with hairpins, tips her hat, and reaches for the music program. Then she studies Claire Pierce across the table. Claire, who has just picked up a remnant of taffeta at two-thirds price and ordered a tidy luncheon, sits cheerless. She has broken with Jimmy, who went back to Kansas City last night. Richardson turns household economy into narrative.
62815-ye-lyttle-salem-maide-a-story-of-w:
Pauline Bradford Mackie wrote Ye Lyttle Salem Maide, a story of witchcraft published at Boston in 1898. Mackie had earlier written a tale of Valley Forge. Hamilton illustrated the book, which uses old-style spelling in its title and chapter heads to match its setting in colonial Salem.

The story turns on Deliverance, a little maid caught in the witchcraft panic. Chapters bring a yellow bird, demons in the meeting-house, the town beadle, and a trial. Abigail sees Deliverance, Cotton Mather visits her, and the road leads toward Gallows Hill. A fellow of Harvard and a great physician enter the tale as well. Mackie writes for young readers, softening a grim chapter of New England history into a story of one child's peril and rescue.
63975-tydore-s-gift:
Tydore's Gift is a science fiction story by Alfred Coppel. It first reached print in a magazine called Planet Stories in September nineteen fifty one, the hosted note says. Its headnote warns that the tower dwellers of a dead world are unpredictable. Old Tydore placed a priceless gift in the greedy hands of one he hated, it says.

Marley walks by a still black canal at nightfall on Mars in the opening. Hoarfrost crunches under his feet, and thin wind whispers over the sand. Earth hangs low in the sky like an emerald pendant. He pulls his silks and furs closer against the sharp cold. He hurries toward Tydore's tower on the path. Home, the green planet seems to say to him, and longing rises in him.
65298-the-gift:
Melvin Sturgis wrote The Gift, a science fiction tale printed in a magazine of November 1951. Its hero, Carl Sloan, began as a boy to perform miracles, healing the sick. The world hated him for it, the blurb says, as a man born a thousand years too soon. The tale opens in a tiny court room, where the air is tense. A prosecutor asks leave to trace the childhood of the defendant.

His aim is to show that the man has been of unsound mind since birth. On that plea, he calls the defendant a public menace, not a victim of chance. The first witness, Ida Mae Holk, has known him since he was two years old. She tells how he and his mother came to Elmwood after his father was gone. Sturgis puts a gifted child on trial before a fearful town.
65659-the-incomplete-theft:
Ralph Burke wrote this science fiction story for the magazine Imagination, where it ran in February nineteen fifty-seven. An alien spy from Valdor hides among the engineers at Sahara Spaceport. His name is Torlyn Khy, but the Earthmen know him as Peter Blane, and his disguise has fooled them all.

The ship he means to steal is the Skyjumper, a great sphere built around a new drive. That drive can throw a ship to any point in the galaxy in a blink. With it, Earth would win its war against Valdor in months. Torlyn plans to take both the plans and the ship itself in one night. The catch sits in the title: how does a thief deliver a principle, not a thing?
65876-theft:
Bill Venable wrote Theft, a science fiction story first printed in Imagination in September 1952. Its headnote is a hook: little green men are telling Thompson what to write, and Thompson is sure he has flipped his lid. His psychiatrist agrees, until he reads the stories.

Thompson, an author, pours rye and lights his pipe late at night, deep in a frown of irritated exasperation. He is an expert in the art of frowning, the tale says, and he has drunk and smoked his way through a stuck evening. Then the little green men are simply there, dictating. The story plays the old joke about where writers get their plots, and lands it neatly.
67729-mountain-craft:
Geoffrey Winthrop Young edited a handbook of mountain craft, printed in New York in 1920 with twenty eight pictures. The book is given to the memory of gallant comrades in the mountains, and a long roll of dead climbers follows. Young says the book is for mountaineers, and a mountaineer is any one who likes to walk, read, or think of mountains.

Young owns that he sets small store by handbooks as such. Open air craft, he holds, is learned on the hill. Yet the book gathers the hard won lore of skilled hands on rock, snow, and ice. Rope work, route choice, and rescue stand beside tales of great climbs in the Alps and beyond.
69616-a-teacher-s-gift:
A Teacher's Gift is a book of stories for children, published at Boston in 1857. Its first tale, John in Search of a Place, opens on a cold, bleak night. John has walked all over the town seeking work and found none. His mother is a poor widow, lately kept to her bed by sickness after years of needle-work.

John plans to ask his new Sabbath school teacher about a place when class breaks up. The fire and supper at home are scanty, yet John prefers them with his mother to any rich table. Illustrations mark the tales, including one called A Bad Sign. The gift of the title is a teacher's offering: plain stories of duty, patience, and love for young readers.
70895-notes-on-witchcraft:
George Lyman Kittredge wrote notes on witchcraft for an antiquarian journal. The Davis Press reprinted the paper at Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1907. It first ran in Volume Eighteen of the American Antiquarian Society's proceedings. Kittredge asks readers to view Salem with calm, not heat.

Belief in witchcraft is a human-wide trait, no race free of it, he argues. New England folk did not invent it; they drew it from the old world. The Salem scare of 1692 stands as one brief spell of a long fear. Students gain a cool, broad frame for a dark page of history.
71117-thunder-on-the-left:
Christopher Morley wrote Thunder on the Left, a novel of a man who meets his young self. Doubleday, Page and Company issued it at Garden City in nineteen hundred twenty five. Morley had written Parnassus on Wheels and The Haunted Bookshop. Old Rome held thunder on the left a sign from the gods.

The nursery at home is being done in fresh paper that day. Martin, the father, walks the room as the damp strips go up. Gay Mother Goose shapes dance round the old walls there. Three bob tailed mice prance in that wall train again and again. New paper now hides them, but Martin knows they stay below. As a boy he studied them in bed at first light each day. Grown life lets a man dress when he will, he muses. Gold light on the garden marks those lost free mornings.
72610-the-christmas-gift:
Oliver Optic wrote this Christmas story for little folks, published by Lee and Shepard at Boston in 1868. It belongs to the Riverdale Story Books, as the series page shows at the front. William Adams, Optic's real name, entered it for copyright in 1862 at Boston.

Great times are coming at the house of Lee during the Christmas holidays, the tale begins. Frank and Flora have long looked forward to the season, the first chapter says. Their cousins Henry and Sarah Vernon are to spend a week with them. Christmas itself is to be celebrated, in one of the cheerful holiday tales that made Optic a household name with children.
72655-continental-stagecraft:
Kenneth Macgowan and Robert Edmond Jones wrote Continental Stagecraft, held at New York in 1922. Parts of the book first ran in Vanity Fair, The Century, and more like journals. The book is given to the play writers of America. A note tells how the work was done.

Macgowan spent ten weeks in the spring of 1922 in play houses abroad. He went through France, Sweden, Germany, and lands now in Czech and Austrian hands. Old trips to Paris and London shaped his eye as well. Photos show new stage forms, such as a ballroom in Vienna turned to a stage. The book urges fresh stage craft on home readers.
73331-taken-or-left:
Mrs O F Walton tells a tale for the young in a story issued at New York by Robert Carter and Brothers. Walton was known for Christie's Old Organ and A Peep Behind the Scenes. A front picture shows Salome, the heroine, refusing to part with her Testament.

Salome tells her own story, opening in a home where her mother raised ten boys and mended stockings every Saturday night. Chapters bring lost money, a children's service, a storm, and Salome's first place in service. A robber's cave, great sorrow, and a leap of twenty years fill out the plot promised by the chapter list. Young readers get a Sunday school tale of honesty, faith, and a girl holding fast under hard trials.
74111-kitecraft:
Charles Miller, a manual training supervisor in Los Angeles, wrote this handbook of kite making for the Manual Arts Press at Peoria, copyrighted in 1914. Los Angeles schools had worked his plans for years, ending each season with a great kite tournament. The introduction argues for life like schooling.

Old schools, Miller says, were half monastery and half factory, and children knew it. Kite season brought the shop and the classroom together, and reached boys no other lesson could reach. The whole community took an interest. Plans for making and flying kites fill the book, with the tournament as its crown. A motto verse rides the title page: the north wind is my prancing steed, the bridle is my kite. The book is a manual with a philosophy tucked inside.
74358-aircraft:
Evan John David, associate editor of Flying, wrote a book on aircraft's development in war and peace and its commercial future, published at New York in September 1919. A photograph shows the NC 4 flying boat with its four Liberty engines of four hundred fifty horsepower each. It flew from Rockaway, New York, to Plymouth, England, under Commander A C Read. The picture is credited to Aerial Age Weekly.

David wrote months after the first World War ended, when surplus planes and trained pilots crowded the sky. His question was what peacetime aviation would carry. Scribner's issued the fully illustrated book. It is a founding text of air commerce advocacy.
77023-stick-to-the-raft:
Mrs George Gladstone wrote Stick to the Raft, issued by the Religious Tract Society of London. Gladstone had written Waiting for Sailing Orders and Norwegian Stories before it. A plate called A Mean Action fronts the tale. Contents promise a German setting throughout.

The Raft heads the chapters, and Kosen and Karl Schmidt follow. The Miller's Son, The Promised Holiday, and The Schutzen Fest fill the middle. Saved by the Raft closes the tale where it began. Her first chapter opens in the Fichtel-Gebirge, the Fir Mountains of Bavaria. Four rivers rise there, once fabled rich in gold. Poor folk and a raft carry Gladstone's moral tale.
77262-sea-spray-and-spindrift:
Taffrail, a naval pen name, spins yarns of the sea in a volume issued in 1917 with eight full-page pictures. The opening tale finds Midshipman Tubby Plantagenet stuck on his Arabic phrase book in heavy heat. His ship, the light cruiser Clytia, lies in the Gulf of Oman.

Nine tales make up the book, among them the stranding of the Hoi-Hau, the salvage of the Cashmere, and the escape of the Speedwell. Gun-runners, patrol work, and plain luck at sea fill the other stories. The pictures show torpedo hits, rockets at night, and decks in action. Readers get brisk wartime and peacetime navy tales told from inside the service, with humor as well as danger.
78109-grateful-peter-s-new-year-s-gift:
Grateful Peter's New Year's Gift is Ruth Lamb's tale for children, printed by the Religious Tract Society in the Little Dot Series. Peter Grant, aged twelve, sells baked potatoes in the street. On the last night of the year he battles a snowstorm and takes only three coppers. His home is a poor cellar in Back Potter Street.

Peter lost his father at four and his mother soon after. Old Sally Graham, who minded him, pleaded to keep him out of the workhouse. The short chapters promise an unexpected present, a running-over and glad tidings. New homes close the story. The tract teaches gratitude and trust in the plain style of its house.
78641-swift:
Carl Van Doren, a Columbia professor and leading American critic, published his Swift with the Viking Press in October 1930. A second printing followed within a month. The frontispiece reproduces Swift's bust in St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin, where he lies buried.

Van Doren's chapters name the stages of a hard life: poor relation, dependent, vicar and wit, man in power, dean and patriot. Then come the Traveller of the great book and the king of triflers. Stella's portrait faces the text, a quiet counterweight to the satire. Van Doren writes brisk, humane biography, clearing away legend to show the proud, wounded man who wrote Gulliver and the Drapier's Letters.
79633-a-six-hour-shift:
A Six-Hour Shift is a sea narrative by William McFee, published at Garden City, New York, by Doubleday, Page in 1920. Part of the text had appeared in the Atlantic Monthly in 1917. This edition is limited to three hundred and seventy-seven copies. McFee sailed as a ship's engineer, and his books made the engine room a place of literature.

The tale opens below decks before a watch. The narrator lies still with eyes closed, listening to the rain drumming on the deck overhead and the gurgle of the scupper pipes. He sorts out the ship's vibrations: the rhythm of the dynamo, the hammer of a pump, the rumble and hiss of the refrigerator. A hideous jar breaks in: the fourth engineer, making tea, has dropped the poker. It is five minutes to two. A year has passed since departure from home port, with one or two days of rest.
britannica-1911-delft:
Delft is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town of Holland in South Holland, on the Schie river near the Hague. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred. It is described as a quiet Dutch town of old brick houses and canals lined with trees.

The text points out the Prinsenhof, once a monastery, where William the Silent was killed. That site later became a museum in his honour. The New Church holds the tombs of the princes of Orange. It also holds a grand monument to William and the tomb of Hugo Grotius, who was born in Delft.
britannica-1911-fortification-and-siegec:
Fortification is the military art of strengthening positions against attack. The word joins Latin fortis, strong, and facere, to make, and it implies the making of defences. A boy who shelters behind a fence from snowballs is only using ground. If he puts up a hurdle on his mound and stands behind that, he has fortified his position. The huge article opens with that plain picture and builds a science of war upon it.

Fortification, it says, has two elements: protection and obstacle. Protection shields the defender from the enemy's missiles. The obstacle keeps the enemy from close quarters and delays him under fire. Protection may be direct, a wall or earth rampart thick enough to stop shot. Its value falls as the defender must expose himself to shoot back. From these principles the treatise ranges over ramparts, ditches, sieges and the attack and defence of fortresses.
britannica-1911-theft: Theft, in a brief entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, names the act of stealing. In English legal use the act is most often called larceny, a Norman French term. The entry notes that theft is the wider word. It covers other forms of taking the goods of another person by wrongful means. The rest of the short entry traces the roots of the old English words for thief and steal, and sets them beside kin terms in German, Dutch, and Gothic.
cast-adrift:
T. S. Arthur's Cast Adrift, published in 1873, calls itself a romance of real life. Arthur tells the reader he lifts only part of the veil over city degradation. His scenes of intemperance and vice, he insists, are photographs from fact. An unwelcome babe and a defrauded young mother open the tale.

Edith's secret marriage and her baby set a plot of revenge in motion. Mrs. Dinneford schemes to destroy Granger, the husband, through forged notes and arrest. The shock of his fall strikes Edith on the night her child is born. Arthur follows the cast adrift of the slums, children starved amid Christian America. The novel pleads for radical reform with a temperance preacher's urgency and a melodrama's twists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-krafft:
Adam Krafft was a sculptor born about 1440 at Nuremberg who died in January 1509 at Schwabach, having carved Nuremberg's last famous Gothic monuments in stone. His earliest extant works are the Seven Falls of Christ, Stations of the Cross showing Christ tottering and falling under his cross. They were completed about 1490 and now sit in Nuremberg's Germanic Museum.

The memorial bronze over the Schreyer and Landauer tomb in St. Sebaldus, completed in 1492, shows Christ bearing the cross, his burial, and resurrection against a landscape. Later, at Imhoff's request, Krafft made the famous marble tabernacle in St. Laurence, tapering to its summit with turrets, canopy, and carved figures. It is universally admired as a supreme Gothic creation. His Passion scenes show deep feeling, and native German strength, simplicity, and piety give his art its value.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-supernatural-:
A supernatural gift is something conferred on nature that lies above all powers of created nature. This entry explains the idea: when God made man, he added gifts his nature could not claim, from qualities and dignities to a final goal beyond nature's own perfection. Such gifts come only from God's free goodness and power.

Some gifts are absolutely supernatural, beyond even angels, lifting the creature to a dignity natural to God alone. Others are only relatively supernatural, raising human nature to an angelic state. Man once held both kinds, lost both in the fall, and regained through Christ only the absolutely supernatural ones, summed up in adoption as God's son and heir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theft:
Secret taking of another's property against the owner's reasonable will defines theft in this moral theology entry. Secret here does not exclude the owner's presence or notice during the act. It means only that the crime happens without violence toward him. Keeping or unjust use of another's goods counts equally as theft.

Refusal to restore a pledge, loan, or deposit, and riding a railway without paying a fair fare, illustrate the point. Owner's unwillingness must be essential and reasonable, not mere close-fistedness. Consent, or legitimate presumption of content despite displeasure at manner, removes theft properly so called. Restitution, gravity, and kinds of theft follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-witchcraft:
Witchcraft is treated here as seeking results beyond human power through evil spirits rather than God. Magic and witchcraft blur together, but witchcraft adds a devil's pact or a plea to evil powers. Its usual aims were death for a hated person, love in a desired one, the dead called up, or ruin wished on enemies and rivals. These ends served it in nearly every age.

Old belief held that witches bargained with Satan, renounced Christ and sacraments, and kept the sabbath as a parody of Mass. They honoured the Prince of Darkness, and gained flight, shape-shifting, torment of victims, and a familiar imp. The entry traces the belief through Egypt, Babylon, Hammurabi's code, and Scripture's stern bans, from Exodus and Deuteronomy through Saul at Endor to Galatians and Revelation.
doe-osti-2575473-enabling-secure-and-res:
Final technical report DE-EE0008453, from Virginia Tech under Ryan M. Gerdes and covering January 2018 to September 2024, tackles the security of extremely fast charging for electric vehicles. Charging in minutes, rivaling a gasoline fill-up, requires tight coordination among the grid, the charging station, and the car. Every link in that chain widens the attack surface for all three.

The project argues that ordinary cybersecurity is not enough here. Charging depends on sensing and actuating in the physical world, so cyber-physical security has to be designed in from the start. The team mixed academic and industry researchers across security, learning under attack, grid resilience, wireless power transfer, converter design, and battery management. Their co-design approach treats hardware and software protections as one problem. The goal is charging that gets faster without getting easier to disrupt, spoof, or damage through its own control systems.
doe-osti-2583546-colorado-alternatively-:
Colorado asked what its airports must build before electric and hydrogen planes arrive, and NREL's study answers field by field. Report NREL/TP-5R00-91144, by James Morris, Bhavesh Rathod, Andrew Kim, and five peers for the state transport department's air division, surveys new-power flight statewide. Short-haul electric flight is close enough that chargers, not planes, may be the choke point.

Chapters work through gains, hurdles, and risks, then the tech and power needs: chargers, grid room, and daily ops. Funds and planes of interest get their own sections. Study tools include REopt for on-site energy and demand models for plug loads. Hydrogen paths are weighed beside battery ones. The aim is sequence: which buys an airport should make now, which to stage, and which to watch, so regional flight can go electric without stranded concrete.
doe-osti-2587635-strong-correlation-dmrg:
Steven White of the University of California, Irvine, wrote this final report for award DE-SC0008696, with Kieron Burke as co-investigator. The award ran from September 2012 through November 2024. It was a twelve-year program on the electronic structure of strongly correlated materials. In such materials, electrons interact so strongly that the standard tool, density functional theory, often fails.

The team computed near-exact answers with the density matrix renormalization group. Those answers served as reference truth. They tested density functional theory, proved when it converges, and trained machine-learned functionals. The group also invented localized basis functions called gausslets. A sliced-basis method makes accurate calculations faster. Extended hydrogen systems served as a proving ground for deriving low-energy models from first principles. A new formalism, conditional-probability DFT, aims to sidestep the usual approximations entirely. Open-source software releases carry the methods to other groups.
doe-osti-3004728-hybrid-sofc-turbogenera:
Christopher Cadou, Eric Wachsman, Gregory Jackson, and the University of Maryland team deliver the final report for ARPA-E award DE-AR0001345, dated October 31, 2025. The project ran from April 2021 to July 2025. It developed a hybrid powerplant for aircraft: a solid oxide fuel cell paired with a small turbine generator. Fuel cells promise quiet, efficient electric flight power if they can be made light enough.

The team ran pressurized fuel cell tests in a purpose-built facility. A commercial 10-by-10-centimeter cell from Elcogen was measured on hydrogen at three temperatures and pressures, producing polarization curves for the design models. The hybrid layout recycles anode exhaust through a combustor and turbine to squeeze more work from the fuel. The report closes the award with activities, outputs, and the test record.
letters-on-demonology-and-witchcraft:
Walter Scott wrote his Letters on Demonology and Witchcraft in 1830. John Murray published them in his Family Library series. That series ran to eighty cheap volumes between 1829 and 1847.

Murray meant the five-shilling books to spread good literature widely. Scott's contribution treats ghosts, fairies, witches, and old trials. A later society reprinted the letters for students of folklore. Scott collects strange tales while doubting many of them. His mix of story and skepticism still makes the book lively reading. Scott's Border childhood fed his love of such lore. He treats old wives' tales with a novelist's sympathy.
nasa-tm-19700023633-preliminary-results-:
Sanford G. Jones, John V. Staskus, and David C. Byers of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 electric propulsion conference at Stanford. It gives early results from potential measurements on the SERT II spacecraft. The readings were taken with hot wire emissive probes.

An ion engine can charge a spacecraft and stir the plasma around it. Such fields could disturb the local space plasma, the authors note. Their probes measured the craft's electric potential in flight. SERT II was a test craft for ion propulsion in orbit. Its data showed how an electric engine and its spacecraft interact in space.
nasa-tm-19720008367-an-electronic-circui:
Vernon D Gebben and John A Webb Jr of the Lewis Research Center described this medical circuit in February 1972, as NASA TM X-68001. It watches the waveform of arterial blood pressure. From that single wave, it picks out two key moments in each heartbeat. Those moments mark the start and end of left ventricular ejection. That is the brief push when the heart's main chamber empties into the arteries.

Ejection starts when pressure rises fast as blood bursts through the aortic valve. It ends at the small notch caused by that valve closing. The circuit turns both events into clean timing signals. Those signals let doctors measure ejection time precisely. Computers monitoring the heart and blood vessels can also use them.
our-gift: Our Gift is a small devotional volume published in Boston in 1851 by Abel Tompkins, prepared by the teachers of the School Street Universalist Sunday School. The hosted sample shows library markings, the title page, and the dedication poem only. That poem says what the book is. It offers no inspired thought or borrowed glories. Instead it brings a simple, pure offering wreathed in wild roses. Tears for the early dead mingle with a moral for the living. No story or lesson of the body appears in the sample.
pee-wee-harris-adrift: The hosted sample shows only the front matter of Pee-wee Harris Adrift, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Percy Keese Fitzhugh and illustrator H. S. Barbour, and Grosset and Dunlap published the book in New York in 1922 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. The frontispiece shows Pee-wee rowing his customers to Alligator Island, and contents entries include "Keekie Joe," "Pee-wee Explores the Island," and "The Lookout Sees a Sail."
scenes-and-characters-or-eighteen-months:
Charlotte M. Younge wrote Scenes and Characters, a story of eighteen months spent at a house called Beechcroft. Macmillan issued the fifth edition at London and New York in 1889, with pictures by W. J. Hennessy. Younge had earlier written The Heir of Redclyffe and The Two Guardians, two novels named on the title page.

The preface speaks for the Mohun family, who host the reader for those eighteen months. Light readers, it says, may simply enjoy Lilias, follow Jane's guesses, and share Phyllis's scrapes, with no duty to hunt for a moral. Parents and guardians wanting big plot turns get fair warning that the life shown is quiet and ordinary. One rule guides the telling: feeling left unchecked turns into selfishness.
the-author-s-craft: Arnold Bennett is named as author on a title page that gives no date, place, or publisher in the pages shown. What follows is a list of his works, grouped as novels, fantasias, short stories, and belles-lettres. Novels named include Anna of the Five Towns, The Old Wives' Tale, and Clayhanger. The belles-lettres list includes How to Become an Author and Literary Taste, titles close to the craft named in this book's own title.
the-giant-raft:
Jules Verne wrote The Giant Raft as a tale of the Amazon in two parts, Eight Hundred Leagues on the Amazon and The Cryptogram. Garral and his kin stand at the heart of the first part.

The contents follow the building of a huge raft, the jangada, and its drift down the river from Iquitos past Ega to Manaos. A man named Torres joins the trip with a dark past in his hands. The second part turns on a coded paper that can clear or hang a man. Judges weigh moral and material proofs while the code resists all skill, and the answer turns on a cannon shot and sheer chance.
the-human-drift:
Jack London gathered essays and sketches in this volume. The text follows the 1919 Mills and Boon edition. The title essay sits beside smaller pieces. One covers small-boat sailing. Another tells of four horses and a sailor. A classic of the sea appears. Two short plays close the list. The title essay opens with a large claim. Civilization is a history of wandering. Men wandered sword in hand, in search of food.

London presses the point through examples high and low. A bankrupt gentleman sails to colonize Virginia. A Cantonese laborer signs on for Hawaiian sugar fields. Hunger drives both men, not romance. He calls such movements drifts. They are unplanned, blind, and automatic. They stretch from pre-human ancestors to modern immigrants. Slovak arrivals in Pennsylvania coal mines end his chain.
the-private-papers-of-henry-ryecroft:
The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft opens with an editor's preface on a little-known writer. Ryecroft's obituaries gave his dates and book titles, and at the time that sufficed. The editor, who examined his papers and chose to print this volume, adds the personal detail that points the self-revelation. He first knew Ryecroft at forty, after twenty years of living by the pen. Poverty and circumstance pressed hard against mental work, and no form of literature brought conspicuous success.

Ryecroft reviewed, translated, and wrote articles, with a volume under his name at long intervals. Small earnings above his needs let him see foreign countries. Independent and rather scornful by nature, he suffered from defeated ambition and grim necessity. Yet his spirit was not broken: discipline made him seem calm and contented in ordinary company. The papers were transcribed from the 1903 Constable edition.
the-snow-drop-a-holiday-gift:
Miss Sarah S. Mower published The Snow-Drop, a holiday gift, in 1851. Her preface calls herself misfortune's child. Disease laid its hand on her in early childhood, she writes. It deprived her of a common school education and the world's sweet intercourse. For more than six years she had scarcely been able to leave home.

The book would never have appeared without life's wintry hour, she says. She wrote it to beguile tedious time. Winds in the groves around her father's humble dwelling inspired her. So did songbirds and the ripple of the Androscoggin gliding past. She offers the work to the benevolent public, hoping it may impress moral and religious sentiment. A first poem praises the snow-drop flower for daring to rear its head under threatening clouds.
thrift:
Samuel Smiles published Thrift at London with John Murray in 1892, opening with verses from George Herbert and Robert Burns. Smiles calls the book a follow-on to Self-Help and Character, and says it might even have come first, because thrift underlies both.

His preface ties the right use of money to generosity, honesty, justice, and self-denial. Its abuse breeds avarice, fraud, extravagance, and improvidence. Industry, he argues, must take interest in its own fruits. Readers get Victorian self-improvement teaching that treats saving, spending, and character as one subject, aimed at independence rather than hoarding.
west-wind-drift:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote West Wind Drift, a sea novel set in the days of German submarines. A large steamer, the Doraine, leaves a South American port one bright October morning. About seven hundred and fifty people are on board. Her holds carry grain, metals, rubber, and goods of war.

The first pages stress how mixed the crowd is, with men of finance, trade, and arms from many lands. McCutcheon sets the fast modern ship against the slow caravel of Amerigo Vespucci, who sailed the same seas in 1501. War at sea hangs over the whole trip. Readers start a long ocean tale of peril and chance.
